title: Never alone
hookLine: when you shut the door and darken the room, you're not alone: God is within, and your own spirit (Discourses 1.14)
carry: a guardian spirit who never sleeps

cards: Late at night, door shut, lights off, phone face down. Nobody can see you.
This is the hour when people eat the thing they swore off, send the message they'll regret, or lie awake feeling more alone than they've felt all day.
It feels like the one hour that doesn't count, because no one is watching. Epictetus told his students that the dark room is never as empty as it looks.

teach.b: This is Discourses book one, chapter fourteen. A student asks: can a person really believe God sees everything they do? Epictetus answers with the whole world.
Everything is bound together. Plants bloom and bear fruit in their season, as if at a signal. Living things change with the moon and the sun.
If plants and our bodies are that closely linked to the whole, how much more our minds, which for the Stoics are pieces of the same reason that runs it all. Then the image.
God has set beside each person a guardian spirit, a daimon, who never sleeps and can't be fooled.
So when you've shut your doors and made it dark inside, never say you're alone. God is within, and your own spirit is within, and they need no light to see what you're doing.
For the Stoics, God isn't only someone peering in from outside; God is also the reason in you, never off duty.
The chapter ends with a soldier's oath.

Soldiers swear loyalty to the emperor, Epictetus says; we should swear one to God too, never to disobey and never to find fault with what we've been given. A neighbor tradition has its own words for the dark.
A psalm in the King James words says, "If I say, Surely the darkness shall cover me; even the night shall be light about me." The two aren't the same teaching, and each is held on its own terms.
In the psalm, darkness hides nothing from God. In Epictetus, the witness is already inside the room.

how: Some readers of Epictetus use this chapter as a nighttime reminder, treating the private, unseen hours as just as real as the public ones.

o: God and your own spirit are with you, even in the dark
a rule never to spend time by yourself in a room
a promise that friends will always stay by your side

games.q: you've shut the door and turned off the light. no one can see. what does Epictetus say to remember?
o: never say you're alone: God is within, and your spirit.
games.why: he says God and your guardian spirit are within, and they need no light to see what you're doing.

practice: If you can, close the door and dim the light, and notice the feeling of being unseen.
Then, in whatever way fits what you believe, notice that you're still here with yourself: the part of you that watches, that knows what you're doing, that never quite switches off.
Sit in that company, with nothing to hide from it and nothing to perform for it.

wordCard.voice: Never alone. Epictetus' reminder for the dark room: God is within, and your own guardian spirit, and neither needs light to see.

orig.note: Greek daimōn: a guardian spirit; Epictetus says God set one beside each person, and Socrates spoke of his own inner sign (daimonion).

carryVoice: Your line: a guardian spirit who never sleeps. The dark room is never empty. Four hundred days, and counting.

sources.ref: Discourses 1.14 (that the deity oversees all things)
